title: Memory controllers and AMBA
summary: Memories are reached through buses. This topic explains what a **memory controller** does, how memories sit in an SoC behind an interconnect, and gives a high-level map of Arm's **AMBA** protocols — APB, AHB, AXI, AXI-Lite and AXI-Stream — with their handshakes. It ends with a small APB memory controller in SystemVerilog.
objectives: List the jobs of a memory controller and compare SRAM and DRAM controllers.
Describe how memories, controllers and bridges sit on an SoC bus.
Name the AMBA protocols and their typical uses.
Read an APB transfer and an AXI VALID/READY handshake.
Read an APB slave that controls an SRAM.

blocks.md: Processors and DMA engines do not drive memory pins directly. They issue **bus transfers** — *read 4 bytes at 0x2000_0A4C* — and a **memory controller** turns them into memory operations. Its jobs:

rows: bus handshake ↔ en / we / addr / din / dout of the RAM
byte address → bank, row, column, byte strobes (Topic 3)
several masters want the same memory: who goes first?
the memory is slower than the bus → stretch the transfer
a 64-bit bus on a 32-bit memory, or bursts of 8 words
open and close rows, refresh, timing rules such as tRCD, tRP
blocks.caption: Jobs of a memory controller

tabs.label: SRAM controller
tabs.md: Simple: one bus transfer = one memory access. Often only a protocol bridge with an address decoder, byte strobes and perhaps one wait state.

tabs.label: DRAM controller
tabs.md: Complex: requests are queued and **reordered** to hit open rows, refresh must be inserted every few microseconds, and a **PHY** handles the high-speed DDR signalling. Covered in *DRAM and External Memory*.

blocks.caption: A typical structure: masters, an AXI interconnect, memory controllers and an APB bridge

blocks.md: Masters (CPU, DMA) start transfers; the **interconnect** decodes the address with the system address map (Topic 3), arbitrates between masters and routes the transfer to the right **slave**. Fast memories sit on the high-performance bus; slow peripheral registers sit behind a **bridge** on a simple bus.

subsections.title: The AMBA family at a glance

blocks.md: Most SoCs use Arm's **AMBA** (Advanced Microcontroller Bus Architecture) protocols. They are free to use and supported by every EDA and IP vendor.

rows: simple, unpipelined: setup + access phase; PREADY for wait states; PSTRB (APB4)
pipelined address and data phases, bursts, one transfer at a time
5 independent channels, VALID/READY handshakes, bursts up to 256 beats, IDs and out-of-order completion, many outstanding transactions
AXI handshakes without bursts or IDs — single 32/64-bit transfers
blocks.caption: The AMBA family

blocks.prompt: Practice: order by complexity, simplest first.

steps.title: APB transfer
steps.md: A **setup** cycle with PSEL = 1, then an **access** cycle with PENABLE = 1. The transfer completes when PREADY = 1; a slave holds PREADY low to insert wait states.

steps.title: AXI handshake
steps.md: On every AXI channel the source drives **VALID** and the data; the destination drives **READY**. A beat is transferred in every clock where both are 1 — either side can stall.

blocks.title: More in the AMBA trainings
blocks.md: The full protocols — all APB, AHB and AXI signals, bursts, IDs, responses and interconnects — are taught in the *AMBA* trainings of the Interfaces topic, each with labs.

subsections.title: In SystemVerilog: an APB slave in front of an SRAM

blocks.md: The smallest useful memory controller: an **APB4 slave** that maps the bus onto a word-addressed memory with byte strobes, and answers bad addresses with an error. The SRAM read is started in the setup phase, so no wait state is needed:

items.title: Where is the address mapping?
items.md: `widx = paddr[AW+1:2]` drops the byte bits (Topic 3); `bad_addr` checks that the upper bits are 0 inside this slave's region.

items.title: Where are the byte strobes?
items.md: Each of the four byte lanes is written only when its `pstrb` bit is 1 — the byte enables of Topic 5.

items.title: What would need a wait state?
items.md: A memory with read latency 2, or an ECC decoder with a pipeline register: the slave would hold `pready` low for one extra cycle.

questions.text: Which are jobs of a memory controller? Select **all** correct answers.
options: Converting bus transfers into memory operations

questions.text: Which bus is typically used for slow peripheral registers?
Which AMBA protocol has no addresses at all?
When is a beat transferred on an AXI channel?
options: In a clock where VALID and READY are both 1

questions.text: How does an APB slave insert a wait state?
options: It keeps PREADY low in the access phase

questions.text: Why are peripherals usually placed behind an AXI-to-APB bridge?
options: APB is simple and cheap for slow registers; the bridge keeps them off the fast bus

questions.text: In apb_sram, an access outside the memory's region returns PSLVERR = 1 in the access phase.
